Time to do so is more than ample, the fact that he has already sent his officers from his command, including his deputy, over there and that all this time he has not yet received a report of his command being implemented, then it would be urgent for him to go there because the presumption would be that all his officers are dead if they hadn't reported back in so long a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in a situation when he was first informed about the incident at 4.45 a.m. and then at 6.50 a.m. he is informed about the attack of the 3rd Battalion, does he then at 4.15 [as interpreted], or rather should he then at 1415 go to Belgrade to see the federal secretary? 1415 hours for the sake of the transcript. Can he simply leave his area of responsibility and go to see the federal secretary without having checked first whether the attack had indeed been stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is highly unlikely that he wouldn't have checked. He should have checked within minutes, or let's say within half an hour after issuing an order to cease-fire. He should have already received a report back whether that is the case or not. If he would not receive such a report, then his personal visit to the battalion should have taken place within the hour of issuing the order, not within six hours. But certainly, in my opinion, he couldn't have travelled to his superior to explain what happened without having checked the facts, without having checked that the shelling had indeed stopped and without checking why it even came to the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if the commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector sent four high-ranking officers with the task of stopping the attack of the 3rd Battalion, through -- if he has communication with them through the forward command post and the communications centre about everything that is going on, is it possible, then, that four colonels cannot stop one captain who is out on an attack?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A highly unlikely situation. However, I have to note, I don't have personal knowledge of this; namely, I don't know which subordinate unit, who precisely, and how much ordinance, in fact, was used. Perhaps this was wilfulness on the part of a level below the battalion commander, and perhaps the battalion commander himself was unable to control his units. Since I don't have this information, I cannot give you an answer. But in any case, a battalion commander would have to be able to be stopped by four higher superior officers, including a deputy superior commander. I don't understand personally how this would be possible, that he could not be stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, let us eliminate this possibility, too, that the subordinates of the battalion commander were the reason for the attack that he took on his own initiative. If this wilful attack starts precisely under the command and by the commander of the 3rd Battalion, and four officers, including the Chief of Staff of the 9th Military Naval Sector, are there where he is, as a high-ranking, experienced officer, do you find this to be possible? Do you understand this situation, that four colonels cannot stop the attack of a battalion that is led by a captain?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a case, the number of colonels with the battalion commander does not matter. What matters is if the deputy VPS commander was there, because the deputy VPS commander can issue an order on the part of the VPS commander. And in this way, he himself can take over command over the units subordinated to the battalion. That, of course, has to be communicated officially. But it is within the remit of the deputy VPS commander. That is most important. And my answer to you is no, I don't understand how this was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If among these four colonels there is the Chief of Staff of the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector and the assistant commander for land forces who is otherwise in charge of that 3rd Battalion, in charge of following that 3rd Battalion, is that, then, the situation you talked about a few minutes ago, that they do have the authority to stop the attack, to replace the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff that is at the same time a deputy commander, that is certainly the case. He can take over command. As for the deputy for the land forces, well, here I can't say at this moment whether he can do so or not. But it depends on whether he had the right to command over land forces. He could have had that or he could not have had that. And thirdly, the term -- I wouldn't use the term "to replace the officer," but what the deputies can do is they can take over command. That is the right term to be used here. And then the officer taking over command is the one that issues the kinds of orders he wants to. The first order of that kind would be, of course, to stop the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, everything I asked you about in relation to this situation on the 6th of December involving various circumstances related to a cease-fire agreed upon on the 5th of December verbally and the signing of the cease agreement was supposed to take place on the 6th of December. On the morning of the 6th of December, there is an unplanned attack and conflict that was not ordered between the 3rd Battalion and the 472nd Brigade and the Croatian side. And in a time span from 4.45 a.m. when the first information about the incident was received until 1415 hours on the same day, when the commander of the military naval sector went to Belgrade to see the federal secretary, in such a situation, in your opinion, according to the system of command and control, and therefore having communications available, vehicles available, a sufficient number of high-ranking officers, including the commander of the 9th VPS, was it realistic, or rather would it have been realistic for such an impermissible attack to be stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within such a time frame, this would absolutely have to be possible, and also implemented. Obviously certain other circumstances arose which allowed for this not to happen, but I'm not familiar with those other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to distribute a document, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, in your report and in the answers that you provided so far, you spoke of the 2nd Operational Group as a formation of a temporary nature with limited authority enjoyed by the commander, and also you raised the fact that you did not see the order of the establishment of the 2nd Operational Group and that, therefore, you could not speak of his exact responsibilities and authority. And in this order, these responsibilities and authorities should be specifically pointed out. Also, you assumed on the basis of the documents you saw, that is to say, of the 9th VPS and the 2nd Operational Group, that there was no interference in the command of the units of the 2nd Operational Group; that is to say, that the 2nd Operational Group had no outside interference coming from other commands, if I understood you correctly. Was that your position?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, concerning the interference of other commands, I didn't discuss that issue. But I would say there was no interference from other commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you now please look at this document, read it, and -- to tell me what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order by the command of the 9th VPS dated 12 October 1991. This order concerns the ceasing of the blockade of the Port of Dubrovnik. The order was addressed to the 16th Border Naval Detachment and was also copied to the operational centre of the 2nd Operational Group. The comma stated here between the operational centre and the 2nd OG is probably a mistake. With this order, the signature of Admiral Jokic orders the 16th Naval Border Detachment to, on 11 October 1991, as of 1800 hours, it ceases the blockade of the Port of Dubrovnik. The next two items state that the detachment need only --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my apologies for interrupting you, we do not need to read on now because the document has been distributed to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me, I would just like to inquire through the Chamber if this document has been exhibited previously and has been put to Admiral Jokic and put into the case through Admiral Jokic. If not, I would object to any use of such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document has not been tendered so far as an exhibit. And it has not been shown to Admiral Jokic during cross-examination. However, what the Defence did do was to base some questions on this document, both to Admiral Jokic and to other witnesses. Here is an expert witness who is perfectly able to interpret the substance of this document in relation to the position put forward by the Defence. Even Admiral Jokic in his interview made direct reference to the substance of this particular document. It was only later that the Defence team managed to get our hands on this document. Otherwise, we certainly would have shown it to Admiral Jokic had we had the document in our possession at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it your proposition, Mr. Rodic, that you didn't have this document when you were cross-examining Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And yet I understood you to say that you had put some questions to him based on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, his interview contains the same thing, and it is his interview that I am about to use where he speaks about what precisely he ordered on the 11th for the blockade to be lifted, of Dubrovnik. This is on page 86 of the B/C/S and on page 92 of the English. I'll read it out to you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no need to do that. How did you come to get the document when you did?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, through our investigators. The document was submitted to us later on. Had we had the document at the time, certainly there would have been no reason for us not to examine Admiral Jokic in relation to this document, since this is a crucial matter. There would have been no reason for us not to put this document before Admiral Jokic. We certainly would have done so had we had the document at the time. There were questions that we asked to Admiral Jokic as a witness in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Respectfully, this document cannot go in. The issue was not even put to Admiral Jokic during the course of his cross-examination. And this aspect of putting the case has been, it appears, deliberately left out with the element of trying to push in a document after the witness is not here, which would be -- which the -- the central issue of which could have been raised and explored very thoroughly and it was not. I think that this was a completely inappropriate attempt to circumvent that rule which is fundamental for cross-examination and that it is inappropriate to even consider the witness looking at this document, let alone if there should be any further motions considering its tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour, it's under Rule 90(H), just for the record. 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, I do not appreciate, Mr. Rodic, what you claim to make of the document and what it is that you seek from the witness about it, nor at the moment do I have a personal recollection of whether this issue was put to Admiral Jokic without the document during his evidence. I understand you to say it was, and Ms. Somers to say it was not. I would ask counsel to resolve that difference between them over the break, which we will now take, because it is material to any ruling on this matter. And it was either referred to or it wasn't. So instead of just assertion one way and the opposite, could the matter be resolved, if necessary by reference to the transcript. And when we return, or perhaps now, Mr. Rodic, you might tell me what you see to be the materiality you wish to get from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the expert witness who wrote his report focussing on the 2nd Operational Group, its temporary nature, saying that it was a military formation of a temporary nature, the Defence, may I remind you, asked questions of Admiral Jokic, even tendering certain documents into evidence through the admiral, because in the organisational chart he omitted some of the units that were in fact under his command. So the Defence insisted that he name all units under the 9th VPS. Therefore, the military naval sector -- the military naval district under whose original command the military naval sector was, did it still have influence over the command exercised over the units of the 9th Military Naval Sector, although the 9th Military Naval Sector was temporarily detached from its military naval district and attached and resubordinated to the 2nd Operational Group at the time. I will remind you, if I may, that Admiral Jokic himself spoke about the enormous tasks he faced and the problems that he had in organising the units of the Navy, moving them from Croatian territory and receiving them in Montenegro, whereas the 2nd Operational Group had no such task and no such objective. The military -- the 2nd Operational Group was not involved in this task. And he didn't have that particular problem. Therefore, the question would be related to the relationship between the military naval district and the military naval sector while under the command of the 2nd Operational Group. And may I remind you, my learned friend and colleague during examination-in-chief introduced a document which was an order by the military naval district describing the task of the 9th VPS in relation to the blockade of Dubrovnik and the main road, the main coastal road. I'm talking about P199. The Exhibit Number is P199. Therefore, the OTP also dealt with this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to me, with respect, to be a terribly long way from your case about the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade on the 6th of December to be concerned about effective control of a naval unit of which we have heard nothing on the 12th of October, 1991. With that thought, we will now adjourn. And I will look for the answer to the difference between you when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I still owe you an explanation from before the break. The position of the Defence, as I have said before, is that the military naval sector under the command of Vice Admiral Jokic contained a parallel command, not only in relation to the 2nd Operational Group, but also to the military naval district within whose original composition the 9th Military Naval Sector had been in much the same way as my learned friend and colleague has shown documents that other witnesses may not have seen. P199 is a similar document of that kind which was tendered through this witness and shown here for the first time. In much the same way, the Defence wishes to ask this witness about that and show him a document that is material to the Defence case. As for the testimony of Admiral Jokic, on cross-examination the Defence asked questions about the relations between the 9th VPS and the military naval district. Among other questions, there was one about the sending of regular combat reports and other documents. Except for the 2nd Operational Group, those reports were also being sent to the military naval district. Furthermore, there were questions about whether units of the 9th VPS had carried out tasks assigned them by the military naval district between the 1st of October and the 31st of December, 1991. So that's why the Defence would like to examine the witness in relation to this document as well as present our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, do you say that this document supports the evidence of Admiral Jokic or contradicts him?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question is in relation to which -- part of the testimony. Some parts confirm his allegations, but some parts contradict his allegations. For example, Admiral Jokic emphasised his obligations during the evacuation of the remaining parts of the military naval district. He had received instructions from the command of the military naval district, so this document is in line with what he told us. This is an order by the military naval district, and he referred to this very order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, there is a distinction between P199. It was sought to be introduced simply because it was a footnoted reference, and nothing more. So we ask the Chamber to take no more note of it than for that purpose way. Secondly, there is no way to authenticate this particular document except through Admiral Jokic, who had spent some four or five days on cross-examination. This issue -- and I apologise, we have in the time allotted attempted to do as thorough as is permissible by time a search, and our recollections are that this issue was not dealt with on cross-examination. We will attempt, if it will assist, attempt to do more searches but in a better time. But that the provisions of Rule 90(H) require -- it is not permissive language, shall put to the witness the case. And this was not put to the witness, with ample opportunity, in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're slipping there between a particular document and the case. The two are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Chamber's inquiry as to whether or not the evidence is contradictory to Admiral Jokic's testimony triggers the requirement that the issue and the document be put to -- certainly the issue be put to, and if there is a subsequent document, the only person who can possibly address its authenticity, of course, is Admiral Jokic. But the issue was passed by. And if it was of such significance, it did not appear to have made its way into that limelight. It would be highly prejudicial at this time to pursue this or allow it to be pursued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, my difficulty with that proposition is my difficulty seeing the force of this document to anything of real significance in the case at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate Your Honour's pronouncement, and I hear Your Honour. At this point, it's the question really of he provisions of 90(H) and what is to be done so we at least preserve the argument. But we believe the document should be given no effect, should not be pursued with this witness, and it is inappropriate to go even further with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You would say that any document that comes to hand after a particular moment in the trial cannot be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. But it must be dealt with in the correct manner, and if it requires a corrective means through an appropriate witness, that's something else. But that is not what is being done now. This is not the appropriate witness. And there's no foundation for this document to even be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your objection firstly is to authenticity. Beyond authenticity, your concern is that the subject matter was not raised with Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The subject matter was not raised to the best of our recollection, and that we do not really know when the document came into the hands of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Counsel has indicated that. You sound too much like opposing counsel objecting to some of your actions earlier in the trial, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I must make the record as -- Your Honour knows that. But I am very concerned that this should be raised at this -- in this manner, and I think it truly is a 90(H) violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may address the issue briefly in relation to this document. My learned friend and colleague says that document P199 was used in relation to a footnote from the original reports. And I'm able to point out where this witness used it. The question was whether the 9th VPS was directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group. That's question C on page 17 of the B/C/S version of the report. And then straight after, in answer to an OTP question, B, on -- D on page 18, this document is again used in answer to the following question: "The VPS in peacetime was subordinated to the command of the military naval district." Was the VPS subordinated to the command of the military naval district also between the 1st of October and the 31st of December, 1991, particularly on the 6th of December 1991? The circumstances were the same, the questions were the same by the OTP. And that's why the Defence is now showing this document. Of course, I will ask the witness to look at the elements contained therein and to interpret them, whether it meets the requirements for being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, are you able to put a date on the time when this first came into the hands of Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know the exact date. It was certainly after Admiral Jokic's testimony. Following Admiral Jokic's testimony, the Defence team has obtained other pieces of evidence which certainly could be put to him, but will be put to other witnesses that the Defence will call in our case. The same applies to the time problem in relation to cross-examination. We had a strict time limit. Therefore, we were not able to put forward some of our evidence that we had planned. However, that does not apply to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. The difficulty with this document is twofold: The difficulty, first, that its author is on the face of it Admiral Jokic, but it was not put to him. And it is said to be a document which in part or which contradicts in part his evidence on a particular issue. The explanation for that omission is said to be the fact that for the first time the document came into the hands of the Defence after the admiral had completed his evidence. We are not told from where or why it was not in their hands earlier. The second level of difficulty is with the relevance of the document. The proposition to which it is said to be relevant is the degree of accountability in a formal military sense of the 9th Military Naval District to the 9th Sector, at least in the period October to December. Relevant to that is said to be this document dated the 12th of October, which shows some relationship or accountability, it is submitted, to that sector. While that has some relevance, perhaps, to credit, and in the view of the Defence, some relevance to their case, the force of this document for that purpose is anything but clear. Without an explanation from the author of the document on its face it is capable of more than one understanding and interpretation. Further, with respect to the view of the Defence, it is not presently apparent that this issue can have any significant materiality to the Defence case as it has been developed. As I understand the Defence case, among other things, no naval units were involved on the 6th of December, which is the material date; what may or may not have been accountability of 9th VPS to the naval sector may be a very interesting question, but it seems to have nothing to do with the shelling of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December. And in those circumstances, I am not persuaded that it would be appropriate to allow a relaxation of the normal rules in respect of cross-examination. So I'm afraid the answer, Mr. Rodic, is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just have a brief clarification, please. If you remember...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: ... pointed out to me that in something I said I may have apparently given the impression that I put the sector as above the district, rather than the other way around. That was unintended. Now, Mr. Rodic, you were saying something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is quite correct that the document was signed by Admiral Jokic. If the established practice is that Admiral Jokic should be the one to confirm the authenticity of this document and that the document should be tendered into evidence through him, I would like to remind you of the situation with a report dated the 9th of December, 1991 that was sent to Admiral Brovet. That was tendered by the OTP as an exhibit, and it was assigned a number when the witness Per Hvalkof was before the Chamber. There are many other such documents, Your Honour. Does that mean that there is a difference of opinions on that, too, and a difference of attitudes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I sought in my comments to make clear that there were two levels of difficulty. One of those was authenticity. That may have been able to be cured by the witness here or some other witness speaking on the apparent effect of the document. But I have not allowed that issue to be pursued because of my concern about the relevance and weight of the document to any issue that is really material in the case on the other side. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence believes that the question of relevance of this particular document is material to our case and to our proposition, which is the proposition addressed by the witness. In answer to questions by the OTP in his report, had he not considered it material, probably he would not have dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, deal with the issue if you haven't already. I'm sure you'll be able to deal with it without this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we resume, may I please have instructions from the Chamber to see what the Chamber feels about the duration of my cross-examination of this particular witness. Does the Trial Chamber expect my cross-examination to be completed today, if I may please have further instructions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Shall we say our prayers may have been in that direction, Mr. Rodic. If you need to go over for a little time in the morning, that will be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll comply with that. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, I will now read out to you from page 278 of the B/C/S a portion of the interview by Admiral Jokic. That's page 305 in the English. I will just read out a passage to you that is material to our line of questioning. Admiral Jokic states: "So, I was near Dubrovnik throughout, even with combat operations going on, my task, which was by no means an easier one, but rather a more difficult task occasionally was to evacuate the entire navy from as far as Slovenia to as far down as Dubrovnik. No one gives me any credit for that, not the 2nd Operational Group, not the General Staff, nor you right now as we speak," speaking to the investigators. That's one thing. And the other thing which I wish to show you is on page 86 of the interview dated September 2003, page 92 in the English. Admiral Jokic stating the following with determination: "On the 11th of October, I had suspended the blockade of Dubrovnik." General Zorc, in your report on page 17 of the B/C/S, the chapter is in the special part of your report, "IV. Command and control," item (c), you provided the following answer to the following question: Was the 9th VPS correctly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group? And on the following page, under (d), the question was: "In peacetime the 9th VPS was subordinated to the command of the VPO, military naval district. Was the 9th VPS subordinated to the command of the VPO also during the period of the 1st of October to the 31st of December, 1991, and in particular on the 6th of December, 1991?" What I have read out to you from the interview where Admiral Jokic says that on the 11th of October he had ordered the lifting of the naval blockade of Dubrovnik and that in the period under consideration, October, November, and December 1991, he had carried out an enormous task evacuating units of the VPO from as far up as Slovenia to as far down as Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. If counsel is going to read from a document, read from a statement, then the complete context needs to be provided to the Chamber. What counsel has read was: "I had suspended the blockade of Dubrovnik." And further down -- this is about Cavtat, et cetera, et cetera. And you -- and were -- question, to Admiral Jokic: "And were you criticised by the 2nd Operational Group for this sort of thing?" Answer: "Yes. Well, they were not happy about it. They were critical of my conduct." This is -- it is a contextual answer, and it needs to be in contextual framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can my learned friend and colleague just point out the page to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is -- I will address myself to the Chamber, of course. It is the same page, page 92 of the English version, 92 at the bottom of the page. And it's the same thing and it carries over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see that it has any relevance to the nature of my question. "Were you criticised by people from the 2nd Operational Group over that?" Answer: "They weren't happy about it. Yes, they were critical about my behaviour." If that's any help, then yes, I agree to have that read out, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the substance of my question is, based on the reports, based on these allegations, did the VPO exercise any influence or command over the 9th VPS during that period of time also? Or was it the case that the commander of the VPS carried out these tasks related to the evacuation and to the blockade of Dubrovnik on his own and of his own accord?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements of Admiral Jokic about all the task assignments he had carried out throughout this period, as well as the document which I received to review concerning the lifting of the blockade of Dubrovnik indicate that the command and control at the level of the 2nd VPO, the VPS [as interpreted], was very complex. This situation was not in line with the provisions and the doctrine. As I have stated in my answers to a number of questions which were posed theoretically, I emphasised, I stated that the system of command and control in the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia is based on singleness of command. Every unit and one commander -- and its commander will have only one superior. The fact that the VPS had the role for receiving all of the navy forces coming in, then it's not quoted anywhere, this task was only carried out via -- on the basis of the directive of the VPO. At the same time, this same sector had combat assignments of the 2nd Operational Group, as a part of the 2nd Operational Group. And I think that this role, this assignment, was a priority role they had. When combat assignments were carried out with all the incidents -- related incidents, I don't think they should have been involved also in other tasks. Therefore, certain activities connected with VPO as well as he was also working and informing the highest echelons in the armed forces, and he also had to command his unit. And I'd say that this was not in line with the command and control that we had in the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may in relation to the transcript, page 63, line 7, what the witness said was that there existed a very complex relationship in terms of control -- command and control between the VPO and the VPS, which the transcript does not reflect in detail. That much is obvious. Same page, 63, lines 22 and 23, also describing the complex nature of the relationship between the VPO and the VPS, as far as I was able to understand the witness in the Slovene language, he said that the VPS also had a role as negotiator on behalf of the Supreme Command of the armed forces. Could we please have the witness confirm these two propositions in case I am right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, I've emphasised three of the assignments which he had to carry out at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, I am going to read something out to you. Page 33, actually, of the interview of Admiral Jokic from September 2003. That is page 35 in the English version. The question of the investigator is: "Yes, you said that Strugar more or less said you should be the host and you should welcome these people. Therefore, it was actually supposed to be Strugar who was to be their host. That is the question of the investigator. And then Admiral Jokic's answer: "No, no, no. I'm saying that in my view, because he is the commander. However, a telegram came from the General Staff, and I think it was sent to me. Now, whether Strugar proposed this is something that I don't know." Question: "I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand what you were saying." Answer: "Well, I'm saying that this telegram was that I should meet the ambassadors and carry out this task. And this telegram came from the General Staff." Is that one of these levels that you referred to a short while ago, the military naval district, the 2nd Operational Group, and the General Staff, that they directly communicate with the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This is one of the lines up to the VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask for D52, Defence Exhibit D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, have you had the opportunity of seeing this document before when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, I was informed concerning the 11 requests that were made to the defence and post to the defence of Dubrovnik. But I didn't consider this relevant concerning the questions that were submitted to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree. What I'm interested in is the introductory part of this document. It is sent to the operations centre of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the SFRY on the 25th of October, 1991 by the command of the 2nd Operational Group. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the text says: "In agreement with the head of the First Administration, General Simonovic, the text of the proposal was drafted, and it was given to the European Mission and the representatives of the town of Dubrovnik providing them with a deadline until 2000 hours on the 27th of October." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does this introduction state that the General Staff was involved in questions related to the negotiations, or rather, the conditions that are set forth here by the JNA as proposals to normalise life in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And in two ways: First, this list of proposals has been drafted in agreement with the chief of the First Administration. Once it was drafted, it was sent to the chief of the operational centre so that the General Staff received in writing the list of these 11 requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, the MPV organ, that is to say, the organ for moral and political guidance and legal affairs -- I'm sorry. My mind just stopped. The assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs. You were asked about this particular organ and the function of this organ within the command. Is it used for propaganda purposes as well? Could you please give us a brief explanation what the function and the tasks of the organ for moral guidance and legal affairs is.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The organ for moral guidance and legal affairs is an organ which is to be found within the command of a unit. The head of this organ is directly subordinate to the commander of the unit. The main area of activity for this organ concerns the following, the following activities: First, moral guidance, named moral and political guidance of soldiers, of young soldiers, coming as conscripts. Secondly, the second area is, or it was, ideological and political education of officers and non-commissioned officers; that is, the permanent officers. It means professionals of the army. Next, the competence of this body was also the political and social -- dissemination of political and social information in the unit concerning topical events in the country and abroad. Fourth, in the competence of this body was also -- were all activities concerning cultural events and entertainment for the units. Next, the competence of this body was also -- was -- were all the activities concerning the information to media, concerning activities of the armed forces or of that unit, name, in short, PR activities. Next, in the competence of this body was also the analysis of combat morale of the units, in the units under this command. And the measures to be taken in order to ensure the highest possible level of combat morale. And finally, in war, the competence of this body involved psychological and propaganda activity and directed to the units of the other side. And I believe that with that, we've covered all the activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P54, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, in this document dated the 6th of November, 1991, the assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs says in the heading of this document "information about activities and the state of morale in units."

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this pertain to their own units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In such information about the activities and state of morale in the units, is there any propaganda effect that is attempted to be achieved vis-a-vis one's own personnel? If you could look at the content, could you see information that is relevant to the activities of one's own units and the state of morale in these units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact, information concerning the situation in the units should be precise and truthful. It should be information ascertained through quality analysis, ascertained also through high quality and precise reports from subordinate units on their state. The purpose of such information is to inform all units about the broader atmosphere within all the units of a military maritime or naval sector. However, what we have here are very subtle elements, subtle elements of information. The manner of expression, various quali-effective [as interpreted] adjectives cannot only be used to inform the corps of their state and status in their position, but you can also use this to inform about their position on these issues. And that is why, in a combat situation, any activity of this nature is called informing of domestic and international public as well as of one's own units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, in this specific document, for example, if it is said when the enemy units operated, how many shells fell on JNA positions, whether the JNA positions returned fire, whether there were any casualties, whether there were any soldiers who were wounded or killed, the assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs, does he get such information from his command? That is to say, from the reports that arrive from subordinate units which are processed there and collected there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the result of the collection of information by the operational centre of the command, which is then given to the commanders and all the units. And every head of sector then carries out his own competences [as interpreted] on that basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in any case, in the interest of the units -- under their command, or rather, would it be in the interest of the units under their command to give a negative propaganda twist to the facts that I referred to just now, that is to say, the enemy operations, the casualties sustained by one's own units, the soldiers wounded and killed, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that would not be good. It would even be counterproductive because every unit knows at least for itself what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly just deal with another matter. Could the witness be shown P160, the map that is Prosecution Exhibit P160. Could the map please be placed on the ELMO so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, attached to your report, inter alia, is your CV. Is it correct that in 1974, 1975 you graduated from the Staff College of the Yugoslav Army in anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your many years of service, and as a high-ranking officer, I'm sure that you're familiar with working maps that commands keep for their own units.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They applied the system of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, could you please take a look at this map and look to the right of the Old Town. Please look at the map itself. I'm sure you'll find it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, can you see the Old Town there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the map please be lifted now so that we can all see that section. That's right, please leave it there and don't move it from there.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take the pointer. You have one there, on the table. To the right of the Old Town, can you see along the coastline a marking for anti-aircraft weapons?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. The thrust of the report was on command and control, and this is not part of the expertise that was sought. The fact that a person has a background in something does not mean that it is the subject of a particular expert report, and this is simply not the area that we have asked General Zorc to inquire into. I can see no basis for proceeding into an area that is beyond the remit of the expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, cross-examination may properly explore with the witness the case of the other party if the witness can advance that. That's the third limb of the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It can be. I think this, perhaps, is a stretch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll see. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness was shown maps, so -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't put more submissions. I might change my mind, Mr. Rodic. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll hurry up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zorc, could you please use the pointer to show the symbol for anti-aircraft defence if you can see one on the coast to the right of the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pointing to a weapon like that just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pointer is in the sea on my monitor. Can you be a bit more precise in terms of the weapon itself. Fine. Now, is that the symbol for an anti-aircraft weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the left of that position, can you see another symbol for anti-aircraft weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the border with Stari Grad. I can see it. Well, it is similar, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, while you were in the JNA, were you in a position to have such working maps for your own units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the instructions related to working maps in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, according to instructions, according to these instructions, as far as the inclusion of information into working map goes [as interpreted], does it have to be completely corresponding to the form of the symbol and also to the scale of the map and also the level of command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as regards point 79 of the instructions for keeping a working map, the centre of a tactical mark on a working map, is it supposed to correspond to the actual place where an appropriate element is in the field, in the area concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the centre of the tactical mark on a working map which denotes a combat weapon or an element of the combat order and which has a particular geometrical form, must it correspond to the actual place, the exact place where the weapon concerned is, or rather the exact place of deployment of the combat order in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is why a working map is actually kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these marks, in these symbols that depict anti-aircraft weapons, does that mean that the centre of this tactical mark that is shown on the map shows the place and position of the weapon concerned in accordance with the instruction?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that has to correspond to the precise position. But of course, it depends very much on what you asked me earlier; namely, in what sort of situation the map is, what sort of a scale the map is drawn in, and in what scale the symbols are drawn in. Here in this case, the symbols for the cannons are way overdimensioned, very much overdimensioned. Oversized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What I'm interested in is the following: So according to the instructions on drawing and keeping working maps, is it correct that the centre of a tactical mark on a working map is supposed to represent the combat weapon and its position?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It should precisely denote the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any rule that only in the case of anti-aircraft weapons the top of the arrow depicts the position of that weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of this, that only the top of the arrow would denote the position. The question is, of course, what sort of rules were applied by those who were working on these maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map is no longer required. It can be put away. Thank you. Your Honour, bearing in mind the time that you have allotted me, if it would be right to adjourn now, then I would very briefly conclude my cross-examination tomorrow in accordance with your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Rodic. We will adjourn now and resume at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
